Agency language shifts to passive when *not* in control: 'They moved it' (E3: L13), 'Marcus came in above me' (E4: L9).

insights.headline: He reads a live system under crisis and moves resources to the highest-leverage intervention without needing permission or external validation.
insights.explanation: E3: Q3 2019 renewal crisis, model predicted 88% gross retention. 'I put every single at-risk account on a wall. Physical wall. Sticky notes... and I stood in front of it every morning at 7:15 with whoever was in the office and we just went account by account. And we ended at like 94%' (L47-49). He says 'The thing I'm actually proud of from those years' is this wall, not the four promotions (L47). This is highest-leverage intervention: he reads the system (11 people, each with accounts, risk tiers), makes it visible, brings daily focus. Does not say 'I asked permission' or 'my boss suggested.' He sees crisis, builds system, brings whoever shows up. Agency is strongest here: 'I put... I stood... we went' (L47-49). Specificity is high (7:15, 94%). No hedging ('I think'), no deference ('the company decided'). He owns the solution. This is zone-of-genius behavior: reading the highest-leverage outcome and moving it without permission—distinct from his pattern of *needing* to control measurement. Here he is solving for the *system's* crisis, not his own anxiety. He 'loved that wall' (L56). Now has 'a wall now at my own place' (E3: L57), replicating the function. Genius is operational crisis response; the compounding mechanism is that he replicates it even when not in crisis (personal company).

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Work and Career. Under *organizational* crisis (team, company, measurable outcome at risk), he will read the system, make it visible (physical wall, sticky notes, shared metric), and mobilize resources without permission. This is distinct from his anxiety-regulation behavior. He will do this well and will be proud of it. He will replicate this in his own company even when not in crisis (because his company is his to optimize). In a role without crisis or with someone else holding the measurement, he will not mobilize this genius.

candidates.headline: He believes that absence of explicit challenge or resistance from authority figures means acceptance, even permission—and that he must find safety in structures where he controls the terms.

facts.what_happened: Speaker was on a two-year mission in southern Brazil (Paraná region: Londrina, Maringá, smaller places) at ages 19–21.
Speaker was assigned to Paraná, south of Brazil, in cities including Londrina and Maringá, and other smaller places.
The mission lasted two years.
Speaker taught a man named Everton who owned a bakery; Everton had experienced a rough event with his brother; Everton was baptized and remained active; Everton now has children.
Everton sends speaker a message every New Year's, every year.
Every Sunday night, missionaries called in numbers (lessons taught, new investigators, member presents, baptismal dates) to district leaders, who reported to zone leaders, who reported to assistants.
Every Wednesday, a fax arrived at the chapel listing every district in the mission and their numbers. This occurred in 2012.
Speaker was made district leader at approximately eight months into the mission.

Speaker created a grid on the back of apartment door using masking tape, tracking every companionship in the district, every day, every number. Speaker recorded Elder Whitmore's wake-up time daily in marker on the door.
Speaker's district increased from four lessons per week to twenty-six lessons per week with member present.
Speaker's district ranked number one on the fax for nine weeks straight.
Assistant Elder Pacheco told speaker at a zone conference that the mission president had been discussing speaker.
Two weeks before transfer calls, speaker wrote a letter to the president requesting assignment to Ivaiporã, a tiny branch with sixty members where an elder had gone home early.
When transfer calls came through and speaker's name was not called as zone leader, speaker's shoulders physically relaxed.
At Ivaiporã, speaker learned Portuguese, ate dinner with the same family (Irmã Solange) approximately forty times, and ate pastel. Everton was actually in Maringá, not Ivaiporã.
Speaker ran the Ivaiporã branch unofficially; branch president was Irmão Cleber who worked nights; speaker made ward council agenda and did records.
Speaker built a second board on the back of a door using masking tape. Trainer said "Elder, você conta tudo" (You count everything).

candidates.headline: Speaker claims to reject advancement and titles, but manufactures a strategic escape route that preserves his non-promotion as a win rather than an alternative.
candidates.explanation: The speaker writes a letter requesting transfer to a difficult branch, framing it as rejection of ambition ('I didn't want a title, I wanted to work'). Yet the letter arrives two weeks before transfer calls—timing that guarantees the president will have processed the request before promotion decisions. When the speaker is not promoted, he experiences physical relief ('shoulders came down') and interprets it as spiritual confirmation. The alternative reading: the letter is not a rejection of advancement but a pre-emptive control mechanism. By requesting the hardest assignment, he secures the outcome (no promotion) while maintaining the narrative of sacrifice and service. He avoids the explicit rejection of promotion (which would shame him) and avoids the explicit acceptance of it (which would violate the prohibition against wanting titles). The relief on transfer day is real—not because ambition was purified, but because the risky gambit worked.
candidates.narrator_frame: "I wanted to just be a missionary, I didn't want a title, I wanted to work. And I meant it! Like when I read it back in my journal I meant every word, it's not fake." (L40-L42). Also: "I thought at the time that was the Spirit confirming it." (L48)

candidates.headline: Speaker has a rare capacity to extract, track, and act on quantified performance data in real time, and is energized by the visibility this creates.
candidates.explanation: The speaker waited for the fax ('I would wait for that fax'), built a custom tracking board unprompted, escalated his district's output sixfold (four to twenty-six lessons/week), and achieved nine weeks of mission-wide ranking. He repeats the board-building at his next assignment ('I built a board there too'). The precision is exceptional: he recalls exact numbers (26 lessons, 60 members), exact timeframes (8 months to promotion, 9 weeks at #1), and the exact mechanics of the system (Sunday calls → Wednesday fax). His trainer observed 'você conta tudo—you count everything'—not as criticism but as the speaker's signature move. This is not general intelligence or work ethic; it is a specific appetite for quantified comparison and real-time ranking. He is lit up by the fax arrival and by his name on it. The alternative (he just worked hard) doesn't explain the repetition of the board or the waiting-for-the-fax energy.
candidates.narrator_frame: "I got kind of, uh, I got a little obsessed." (L18). Also: "Elder, você conta tudo." (L58, 'meant it as a compliment I'm pretty sure').

candidates.headline: Speaker operates from a belief that visibility and ranking are evidence of worth, and that being seen to count (and be counted) confers legitimacy.
candidates.explanation: The speaker reads results in the bathroom because 'it felt weird to be that happy about it in front of everybody' (L30). This is not shame about ambition—he writes letters requesting hard assignments and builds boards in communal spaces. It is shame or discomfort about the *happiness* of being ranked. He needs the ranking to be real (the fax, the numbers, the grid) but doesn't want to appear to need it. The tracking of Elder Whitmore's wake-up time is instructive: it is precise, daily, marker-on-door accountability—not for Whitmore's benefit (Whitmore laughs but 'I don't think he thought it was funny'), but for the board's comprehensiveness. Every number must be captured. This suggests the speaker believes that what is counted is what counts—that the board's completeness = the district's legitimacy = the speaker's legitimacy as a leader. Absence of a number would be a gap in reality.

candidates.headline: He believes that if he makes a choice with insufficient information or agency, someone else will control the outcome, and this is unbearable to him.
candidates.explanation: In E1, he quits wrestling the night before the wrestle-off—a preemptive choice that removes the risk of being measured by someone else (coach, Tanner, the bracket). He says 'I'd rather be the guy who's building the day than the guy waiting to find out what the day is' (L46), which is not about preference but about who gets to set the terms. In E2, he writes the mission president a letter asking for Ivaiporã *before transfer calls* (L43-44)—a preemptive move that ensures he controls the assignment rather than being assigned. He says 'I meant every word' (L42), but he sent it two weeks early, which is the move of someone who cannot bear to wait and be chosen. In E4, the seed round offer at 'decent terms' (L53) would have meant 'a guy I'd have to call every quarter and explain myself to' (L56-57). He sits in his car for forty minutes thinking about the board seat, not the dilution (which he says was the reason but 'yeah, dilution, sure' undercuts it). He takes 100% ownership at lower salary (L52) rather than 30-40% ownership with a board. In E5, during the NICU crisis when there is literally nothing to control (L15-17: 'there's no plan... you wait'), he builds a spreadsheet and regroutes his bathroom at 2 am. The belief is: *if I don't control it, I will be controlled*. He does not say this. The form of the belief emerges in the pattern of preemption and the anxiety that surfaces when control is threatened (E4: 'felt sick on Wednesdays').
candidates.narrator_frame: He frames these choices as preferences ('I'd rather be the guy who's building the day') or values ('I didn't want a title, I wanted to work' in the mission letter). He does not name the fear of being subject to someone else's judgment or timeline. He says of the seed round, 'I sleep' (E4: L62), suggesting relief, not regret—the relief of not being answerable to someone else.
candidates.form_evidence: Preemption is the signature form: quit before wrestle-off, ask for reassignment before transfer calls, leave job before reorg, build own company before someone else's company. Agency language shifts to passive/external when he is *not* in control: 'They moved it into Salesforce' (E3: L13); 'Marcus came in above me' (E4: L9); 'they call it a — it was a placental thing' (E5: L3-4). When threatened with measurement by others, specificity increases (exact records, exact handoffs, exact rejection of board seat terms) but emotional explanation evaporates. In E5, the only moment he sits without control (NICU, 19 days, no plan), he cannot stay present for six minutes (L39). The regrouting is compulsive behavior under anxiety.
candidates.check: E1: Quits preemptively before being measured. E2: Requests transfer preemptively before being assigned/promoted. E3: Builds own tracking systems when company systems measure him; micromanages CSM when account is at risk. E4: Leaves when new manager above him structures the work; refuses board seat to avoid being answerable. E5: When he has zero control (NICU), he makes spreadsheet and leaves chair after six minutes. In 5/5, the pattern is: when his agency is threatened (by coach not fighting, by assignment without choice, by Marcus's structure, by board governance, by medical event), he either preempts or compulsively tries to regain control. Belief holds.
candidates.counterexample: E3 is the strongest counter: he stays at the startup for five years and accepts four promotions he doesn't choose. He says 'it was just that the company was doubling, like, if you just don't leave and you're not bad you go up' (L11). This appears to show he can accept assignment without preempting. However, his response is not acceptance—it is *capture*: he builds the leaderboard obsession, the spreadsheet tracking CSMs, the sticky-note wall. He is not staying because he accepts the hierarchy; he is staying because he can build a system *within* it that makes the measure visible and operationalizable. The moment Marcus structures the *forecasting* in a way he can't predict or control (forecast calls, questions about every deal), he feels sick (L14-15) and leaves. The NICU shows the clearest boundary: in E5, there is no system to build that changes the outcome. He builds a spreadsheet anyway (L20-25), the nurses don't need it (L24), and he *cannot stay in the chair* (L39). This is the mechanism unmasked: he can stay in a hierarchy if he can build a system that makes it legible. When even that fails, he exits or compulses. The counterexample shows the mechanism is *more specific* than 'needs control'—it is 'cannot bear to be measured by someone else's system without building a parallel system that he owns'. The NICU breaks even that, which is why he describes it as 'the worst I've ever been' (L12).

candidates.headline: He says he values autonomy and hates micromanagement, but systematically micromanages his teams and his marriage through capture and measurement.
candidates.explanation: In E3, he says 'I'm a big believer in autonomy. I really am. I hated being micromanaged' (L20-22), and never did ride-alongs with Doug despite 'legitimate reasons' (L24). Yet in the same experience, he 'took' Kaylee's account off her, telling her it was to help her focus (L31-33), and her exit interview cited 'not being trusted' (L36). He ran every QBR deck himself, rebuilding them at 11:40 pm with 'just a couple tweaks!' (L38-42). He had his own spreadsheet tracking 'every CSM's touches per account per week. Color coded. Nobody asked me for it' (L43-45). In E5, he says autonomy matters ('I really am' a believer, L20), yet Council doc has 'four items: Calendar, money, kids, us' with no space for conversation or mystery (L47-48). Britt notes this: 'you'd rather have a meeting with me than a conversation' (L52). He responds by adding an 'emotional check-in section' to the doc (L54)—systematizing the very thing that cannot be systematized. The gap is: he experiences being measured (Doug's ride-alongs, Marcus's forecast calls) as invasive and leaves. But when he holds the measure, it feels like care or stewardship. What Kaylee and Britt experience as micromanagement, he experiences as protecting the system. The lived version is: *I will not be measured, but I will measure you thoroughly, because measurement keeps things legible.*
candidates.narrator_frame: He says 'I know what that feels like and I don't do that to my people' (E3: L25), which is his direct statement of the value. He does not see the CSM spreadsheet or the QBR rewrites as measurement; he sees them as 'doing everybody's QBR decks' (L38)—as help, as ownership, as keeping the account safe. When Britt points out the meeting-over-conversation pattern, he 'laugh[s]' and fixes the doc (L52-53), suggesting he hears it but does not land on what she is naming.
candidates.form_evidence: Agency reversal: 'I hated being micromanaged' (E3: L22) is strong autonomy language. But 'I took it' (off Kaylee, L31), 'I ran' (the renewal, L34), 'I had' (my own spreadsheet, L43), 'I'd rebuild them' (QBR decks, L40) show consistent seizure of control framed as protection. Specificity increases when he is measuring others ('touches per account per week,' 'color coded,' 'just a couple tweaks!') and when he is being measured ('I felt sick on Wednesdays'). The absence of curiosity about how Kaylee experienced this or how Britt experiences Council suggests he has not integrated their version of events into his sense-making. When Britt laughs hard and cries at the 'emotional check-in section,' he says 'I still don't totally know which kind of crying that was' (E5: L55)—suggesting he cannot read the signal. This is not cruelty; it is a systematic inability to move from measuring to seeing.
candidates.check: E3: Says he hates micromanagement (L20-22); does ride-alongs with Doug (refused, L22-24). Says he 'doesn't do that to people' (L25); tracks CSM touches, rewrites QBRs, takes Kaylee's account (L38-45). Kaylee quits citing 'not being trusted' (L36). Contradiction established. E5: Values autonomy in marriage; proposes Council doc with four pre-set items (L47-48); adds emotional check-in when Britt points out the pattern (L54); cannot read Britt's response (L55). Pattern holds: stated value is autonomy; lived version is structured measurement framed as care.
candidates.counterexample: In E4, when he leaves the startup and owns 100%, he reports not building a board structure around decisions. He takes a salary 'honestly less than I was making' (E4: L51) and refuses a seed investor to keep autonomy (L52-57). He does not micromanage Rodrigo, his contractor in Brazil—he 'hired' him and they 'built' together (L21). This could suggest that he micromanages *down the hierarchy* but not in peer or chosen relationships. However, the stronger read is: he does not micromanage when he does *not need to measure his own performance relative to someone else*. At the startup, there was a leaderboard, a VP above him, forecast calls—external measures. As founder, the measure is inside him (he checks his own numbers daily, but there is no external judge). The lack of board structure is not freedom from measurement; it is freedom from *being measured by others*. He still has the wall (E3: L57-59 compares it to the startup wall). The pattern holds because autonomy for him means 'I set the measure, you don't.' It does not mean 'neither of us measures.'

He takes a salary 'honestly less than I was making at the startup' (L51) and notes 'Britt has thoughts about that' (L51), suggesting relational cost. When the calls come and his name isn't in the zone leader assignments, he feels 'so relaxed' (L45)—not disappointed or frustrated, but *relieved*. Absence: he does not mention ambition, recognition, or status as things he wanted. He mentions them as things others wanted for him (Marcus's process, the seed guy's offer, Britt's worry about salary).

candidates.headline: He collects evidence of his own capability (checking Tanner's record, remembering exact numbers, justifying the quit in retrospect) without integrating the lesson—suggesting he may be stuck in validation loops rather than moving forward from past choices.

He remembers his own record (23-4, second in state tourney) (L8-10) and speculates Tanner's losses to contextualize his own record (L9). Then, near the end, he reopens it: 'I still think I would've beat Tanner... he gassed out, he always gassed out in the third' (L55-57). He is assembling evidence of a counterfactual—that he *could have won*—without asking what the validation does for him. The narrator says 'I'm aware. He has integrated the choice (he is at peace with leaving wrestling, he loves what he did instead), but he has *not* integrated the unchosen path. He still needs to know he could have beaten Tanner. This is not regret; it is unfinished validation.
candidates.narrator_frame: 'I'm aware. I'm aware of when it was' (L20-21) suggests he knows someone might judge the timing and he is preemptively defending it. 'That's a weird thing for a fifteen-year-old to do but I did' (L31-32) notes the oddness without curiosity. 'I still think I would've beat Tanner' is present tense, suggesting the thought returns. He does not say 'I wonder if that choice cost me something' or 'I've made peace with the quit.' He says 'I'm aware' and 'I think I would've'—defensive and speculative at once.
candidates.form_evidence: Repetition of numbers (23-4 appears at L8 and L54) suggests ongoing reference to the same fact, as if saying it again confirms it. Tanner's record is looked up actively (L31-32: 'I actively went and found out') and then returned to speculatively (L55-57). The specificity is extraordinary ('eleven pounds on me,' 'gassed out in the third') in a narrative otherwise sparse on emotional detail, suggesting the exact measurements are what matter. The absence of integration is the pattern: he does not say 'I'm glad I quit' or 'I wish I'd stayed' or 'I've moved past this.' He says 'I'm aware. I still think. I checked.'
candidates.check: Single experience (E1). Pattern is the internal repetition and validation-seeking within one story. Not a cross-experience pattern.
candidates.counterexample: In E4, when he leaves the startup, he does not return to check Marcus's sales record or speculate how the company would have gone if he'd stayed to take the VP role (which 'probably would've gone to Priya'). This suggests that in E4, he has integrated the choice and moved forward. In E1, he has not. The difference may be: in E1, he is still living the consequences in his memory (he checks Tanner's record at some point after the season); in E4, he left before the reorg and is now building, so he has new outcomes to measure. The pattern may be specific to past choices where the counterfactual still looms unsettled.

If he is still collecting Tanner-like evidence about the startup by late 2027, the pattern is active. If he has let it go, the pattern has resolved.

candidates.headline: He can read a room or system under crisis and move resources or people to solve for the highest-leverage outcome, without needing permission or external validation.
candidates.explanation: In E3, during the Q3 2019 renewal crisis, the model predicted 88% gross retention. He 'put every single at-risk account on a wall. Physical wall. Sticky notes, like a giant one, and I stood in front of it every morning at 7:15 with whoever was in the office and we just went account by account' (L47-49). They ended at 94%. He says 'The thing I'm actually proud of from those years' is this wall, not the four promotions (L47). The wall is the one where he reads the system (11 people, each with a set of accounts, each account at a risk level), makes it visible, and moves daily to solve the highest-risk items. He does not say 'I got permission to do this' or 'my boss suggested it.' He sees the crisis, builds the system, and brings whoever is in the office. This is zone-of-genius behavior: reading the highest-leverage intervention and moving it without permission.
candidates.narrator_frame: He says 'The thing I'm actually proud of' (L47), which positions this as his signature accomplishment from those years, not the title progression. He does not frame it as management technique or best practice; he frames it as something he felt good about ('I loved that wall', L56).
candidates.form_evidence: Agency is strongest here: 'I put... I stood... we went' (L47-49). Specificity is high (every morning, 7:15, 94%). This is the inverse of his pattern elsewhere: when he is solving a system problem without needing approval, he is precise, energized, and active. No hedging ('I think', 'I might have'), no deference ('the company decided,' 'my manager said'). He owns the solution.
candidates.check: Single experience (E3: the NICU crisis is similar, but it is solving for his own anxiety, not a system crisis. The startup wall is the clearest case of reading a live system and moving resources.)
candidates.counterexample: In E5, during the NICU crisis, he does not move the system. He builds a spreadsheet for himself and cannot sit with Britt (L39). He is solving his own anxiety, not the system (the NICU staff 'had it all in Epic,' L24). The pattern holds only when he is reading *an external system* (a team, a company, a market crisis), not solving for his own fear. This refines the genius: it is reading others' work and systemic risk, not personal crisis.

evidence.quote: The thing I'm actually proud of from those years — we had this renewal quarter, Q3 of, uh, 2019 I think, where churn was gonna be brutal because of a pricing change, and I put every single at-risk account on a wall. Physical wall. Sticky notes, like a giant one, and I stood in front of it every morning at 7:15 with whoever was in the office and we just went account by account. And we ended at like 94% gross retention when the model said 88.
That wall. I loved that wall.

candidates.falsifier: If colleagues report that the wall was mandated or suggested by leadership, or if he later reports that he asked permission first, this would suggest he is not moving without authorization. Or if the outcome (94% vs. 88%) was achieved despite his system rather than because of it, this would weaken the claim. Test: Ask a colleague from that time period whether he initiated this or was directed to do it.
candidates.would_predict: Work and Career: At the startup, he will continue to rely on visible systems (the wall, the sticky notes, the daily standups) to move his team. If growth requires him to delegate this role to a manager or to move to a more strategic, less hands-on role, he may struggle with the transition. Test him: Ask him to describe his current process for managing at-risk accounts or churn. If he still has a physical or visible system, this genius is active. If he's moved to a tool or handed it to someone else, this genius may be dormant.

candidates.headline: He uses task completion (garage cleaning, bathroom regrouting, spreadsheet building) as a somatic regulation when faced with relational ambiguity or loss of control, and does not recognize these as anxiety responses.
candidates.explanation: In E4, when deciding to leave the startup, he 'cleaned the garage. Like, the whole thing. Twelve hours, both days. Pegboard, labeled bins, I swept the ceiling, who sweeps a ceiling' (L44-47). Britt observes 'She knows what the garage means' (L48), suggesting this is a recognizable pattern. In E5, during the NICU when 'there is nothing to do' (E5: L13-14) and he cannot control the outcome, he first 'made a spreadsheet. Obviously' (L20), then 'regrouted the master bathroom' at 2 am 'on my knees with the little tool, scraping it out' (L27-29). He says 'my mother-in-law was staying with us and I think she thought I'd lost it' (L30). He also 'did the garage again. The garage that was already done' (L31-32). After he cannot sit with Britt (six minutes, L39), he 'went and got coffee for the nurses. Decaf, it's a whole thing, I don't drink it but I got very into being the guy who brought the nurses stuff' (L40-42). These are all behaviors that move from internal dysregulation (nothing to control, no plan, relational request he cannot meet) to external task completion. The task completion is not conscious anxiety management; he reports the bathroom regrouting as something he 'did,' not something he 'needed to do.' But Britt's observation ('she was in the chair... she basically lived in that chair by his isolette' while he regrouted) and the pattern across experiences (garage in E4, bathroom in E5, spreadsheet in both) suggest a mechanism: *when relational or control needs are frustrated, he moves to physical task to regulate his nervous system without naming it as regulation.*
candidates.narrator_frame: He says 'The weekend I decided, I cleaned the garage' (E4: L44), linking the decision to the task without claiming the task *was* the decision-making. He says 'I made a spreadsheet. Obviously' (E5: L20), normalizing it, not recognizing it as a response to crisis. He says 'I got very into being the guy who brought the nurses stuff' (E5: L41), reframing compulsive task-work as a role he chose. He does not say 'I was anxious and I needed to move my body' or 'I was avoiding the NICU by regrouting.'
candidates.form_evidence: Escalation of task detail in crisis moments: in the garage, he specifies 'Pegboard, labeled bins, I swept the ceiling' (E4: L47). In the bathroom, 'on my knees with the little tool, scraping it out' (E5: L29). In the NICU, exact volumes, times, trend lines (E5: L22-23). The more uncontrollable the situation, the more granular the task. Absence: he never reports feeling his anxiety, never names the task as calming, never reflects on the pattern. Agency is displaced: he says 'I did the garage again. The garage that was already done' rather than 'I felt compelled to redo the garage.' The transition from relational frustration to task is immediate and unreflective: Britt asks for presence (E5: L36), he sits for six minutes, he cannot stay, he gets coffee (L40). No pause, no naming of what is happening.
candidates.check: E1: Chooses task (truck work) over relational risk (wrestling, coach's judgment). E4: Makes major decision while cleaning garage; Britt recognizes it as a pattern. E5: In maximum control loss (NICU), escalates to three parallel tasks (spreadsheet, bathroom regrouting, garage re-doing). Britt asks for presence, he cannot stay. Pattern holds: in 3/5 experiences with explicit relational or control rupture, he moves to task.
candidates.counterexample: E2 and E3 do not show explicit task escalation during crisis. In E2, he builds the board and the letter, which are task-like, but they are also his regular mode (he is always building a board). In E3, the wall is a crisis response, but it is also his work—he is solving for the system, not regulating himself. The pattern is most clear in E4-5 when the task is *not* his work and is excessive (regrouting a tile, sweeping a ceiling during decision-making). This suggests the mechanism is specific to non-work, domestic task escalation during relational or control crisis.

evidence.quote: The weekend I decided, I cleaned the garage. Like, the whole thing. Twelve hours, both days. Pegboard, labeled bins, I swept the ceiling, who sweeps a ceiling. Britt came out Sunday afternoon and just stood there and goes, 'So we're leaving the job, huh.' Because she knows. She knows what the garage means.

And one night she said — and she wasn't mean about it, she never is — she said, 'Dallin, I don't need the numbers. I need you to just sit down.' And I said okay. And I sat down. And I lasted, I'm not exaggerating, maybe six minutes. And then I went and got coffee for the nurses.

candidates.falsifier: If he reports a moment where he recognized the pattern (e.g., 'I realized I was regrouting because I was anxious') and chose a different response (sitting, talking, naming the anxiety), this pattern is under change. Or if Britt reports that he has started naming the pattern himself, this would suggest awareness is emerging.
candidates.would_predict: Health and Wellness: During high-stress periods (company scaling crisis, family conflict, medical event), his sleep and rest quality will likely decline, but he will report feeling 'productive' or 'focused' (due to increased task completion). His body may show signs of unregulated stress (tension, cortisol, insomnia) even as he reports feeling fine. Test him: During the next significant relational or work crisis, ask him daily 'What did you accomplish?' and 'How are you feeling emotionally?' If he can list tasks but not name feelings, and if the task list grows daily, the pattern is active. Relationships: Britt will continue to be the external mirror (as she is now) and may experience secondary stress from managing his regulation. If they have another child or crisis, his domestic task escalation may increase, and she may reach a breaking point with the pattern.

candidates.headline: He believes that competence and visibility in a system (appearing on top of a leaderboard, being known for specific outputs) is the same as belonging or being valued, and he is urgently motivated by this equivalence.
candidates.explanation: In E2, he obsesses over the numbers board. 'I would wait for that fax' (L17), and when he goes nine weeks at number one, 'I'd read it in the bathroom because it felt weird to be that happy about it in front of everybody' (L30). This is not just liking numbers; this is confusing numerical rank with acceptance or worth. He says 'My trainer used to say "Elder, você conta tudo." You count everything. He meant it as a compliment I'm pretty sure' (E2: L58-59). The uncertainty ('I'm pretty sure') suggests he knows the counting can be read as pathological, not complimentary. In E3, he checks the Salesforce dashboard at 5:40 am, 'and I'd just want to see it' (L16). It is described as 'the fax again' (L18), which confirms the mechanism: he needs to see himself ranked, confirmed, on top. When he is not visible in a system (the NICU where the nurses have the real system in Epic, his spreadsheet is not needed), he cannot feel value. When he is excluded from the leadership offsite (E4: L34-35), he first rationalizes it ('only VP and up,' L35-36), then says 'two directors went' (L37), then says 'But also I wouldn't have gone' (L39). This is a person checking whether he was valued (on the list), not found, then reassigning his own lack of desire ('I wouldn't have wanted to go anyway'). The belief is not stated, but the pattern is: *visibility in a system, especially one where you are ranked or measured, feels like belonging.* This is different from the earlier pattern about control; this is about *being seen and validated through a system*.
candidates.narrator_frame: He does not name this as a need for validation. He frames it as preference for organization, curiosity about numbers, or natural awareness of how systems work. When Britt points out that he is visible and counted in the Council doc ('Us' is last), he adds an emotional check-in section rather than questioning why visibility in a doc matters. He does not say 'I need to know I'm ranked well' or 'I feel invisible without a leaderboard'; he says 'I'd wait for that fax' and 'I'd just want to see it.'
candidates.form_evidence: Affective language appears only around visibility: 'I felt so relaxed' (E2: L45) when he was not promoted (removed from the visible ranking), then 'my shoulders came down' (L47). But this is relief at not being *in* the ranking anymore, not at being accepted. The opposite emotion should show: he should feel *eager* when moving to the top of the leaderboard, but he goes to the *bathroom* to feel that happiness (L30), suggesting the emotion is confusing or not meant for public consumption. This displacement suggests he knows the belief is not socially acceptable. Absence: he never reports feeling valued by Britt for who he is (his character, his care, his presence). He reports feeling connected in the truck through task, in Brazil through the board, at the startup through the wall. All are systems where he is visible and executing well.
candidates.check: E2: Nine weeks at number one on fax; reads in bathroom (embarrassment at happiness). E3: Checks dashboard at 5:40 am; has own spreadsheet nobody asked for; not on leadership offsite invite (rationalizes, then notes two directors *were* invited). E4: Sits in car for 40 minutes thinking about board seat (which would make him visible as accountable), not about dilution. In 3/5 full experiences, visibility/ranking is a significant motivator. In E1 (wrestling), he checks Tanner's record (comparative visibility). In E5 (NICU), he has a spreadsheet the nurses don't need, suggesting the visibility is for him, not for outcome.
candidates.counterexample: In E4, when he leaves the startup and owns 100%, he is *not* on a public leaderboard anymore. He checks his own numbers (mentioned but not elaborated). The need for external visibility seems to diminish. He has Sam as a point of comparison (E4: L60: 'My buddy Sam took money and he's at eleven') but he does not obsess over Sam's leaderboard. This could suggest that owning the system removes the need for external validation. However, he still has 'a wall now at my own place' (E3: L57), which replicates the leaderboard function privately. So the need for *visibility in a system* remains; he has just internalized the system (it is his company, his wall, his rules). The belief holds, but the manifestation has shifted from needing to be ranked by others to needing to see himself rank within his own system.

evidence.quote: I had a spreadsheet, my own one, not the company one, where I tracked every CSM's touches per account per week. Color coded. Nobody asked me for it. I just wanted to know.

One thing I remember. They did a leadership offsite in Park City in January and I wasn't on the invite list. And at the time I told Britt it was because they were only doing VP and up and I was a director. And that's, that is true, that was the criteria. But two directors went.

candidates.falsifier: If he reports feeling valued or belonging without being ranked or visible in a system (e.g., in a friendship, a hobby, or a relational moment where he is not measured), this belief would be challenged. Or if he stops checking his own numbers at the startup and reports feeling at peace with not knowing, this would suggest the belief is resolving.
candidates.would_predict: Work and Career (undiscussed): As his startup scales, if he brings on a co-founder or board member, he will struggle with shared decision-making and visibility. If the founder gets public credit or recognition while he handles operations, he will feel invisible and potentially resentful, even if his work is valued privately. He may eventually build a role or brand identity (founder, CEO, public speaker) where he is visible again. Test him: Tell him the startup is doing well but ask him to stay behind the scenes (no social media, no founder interviews, no conference talks). Observe whether he feels satisfied or increasingly anxious.

candidates.headline: He is loyal to people and systems he has chosen or built, but abandons those that measure him without his consent—and this contradiction is only visible when both instances appear in sequence.
candidates.explanation: In E2, he is intensely loyal to Everton (his investigator, still sends messages every New Year, L6-9) and to Irmã Solange (ate dinner at her house 40 times, L49), and to Irmão Cleber (the branch president, 'super nice guy', L53). But to the mission system—the one that measures him and ranks him—he preemptively exits by writing the letter before transfers (L43-44). In E3, he is loyal to the startup system (stays five years, builds four systems of tracking) but the moment Marcus creates a *new* system of measurement (forecast calls he doesn't control, L10-13), he feels sick (L14-15) and leaves. In E4, he is loyal to the people he builds with (Rodrigo in Brazil, his nine people at the startup) but will not take on a board member who would measure him. In E5, he is intensely loyal to Britt (stays married, builds Council with her, L46-51) but when she asks him to sit with her emotionally (unmeasured, unscheduled), he cannot stay for six minutes (L39). The compounding insight is this: *his loyalty is to systems and people where he is in control of the measurement or where there is no measurement. The moment measurement is imposed from outside, he experiences it as a betrayal, and loyalty vanishes.*
candidates.narrator_frame: He does not name this as conditional loyalty. He says 'I meant it!' about the mission letter (E2: L42), suggesting genuine commitment to the choice. He says 'I really am' a believer in autonomy (E3: L20), suggesting his loyalty is to autonomy, not to people. He does not say 'I was loyal until you measured me, then I left.' He says 'I wanted to work' or 'I wanted to own it' or 'I sleep now.'
candidates.form_evidence: Emotional language shifts: with Everton (chosen relationship, no hierarchy), he uses 'amazing' (E2: L9) and 'friends on Facebook' (E6). With Marcus (external measurement), he uses 'felt sick' (E3: L14). The form of loyalty is task-based: he brings coffee to nurses, he builds systems, he eats at Irmã Solange's house repeatedly. But the moment the task is imposed rather than chosen (Britt asks him to sit), he cannot perform. Absence of anger: he does not say 'Marcus was unfair' or 'the mission president betrayed me.' He just leaves or preempts. This suggests he does not experience it as interpersonal rejection; he experiences it as a systems mismatch.
candidates.check: E2: Loyal to Everton (chosen), Irmã Solange (chosen), Irmão Cleber (chosen); preemptively exits the mission promotion system. E3: Loyal to the startup system while he can build within it; leaves when Marcus creates external measurement. E4: Loyal to Rodrigo; will not take board member. E5: Loyal to Britt in structured moments; cannot sit with her unstructured request. Pattern: loyalty *to systems and people he controls or chooses*, not to hierarchies that measure him. Compounding: this only becomes visible when E5 shows the same pattern apply to marriage, which is his deepest commitment—suggesting the mechanism is foundational, not contextual.
candidates.counterexample: In E3, he stays at the startup for five years under the company's measurement systems (leaderboard, forecasts, promotions). He does not immediately leave when the leaderboard appears or when he is promoted. But his response is to *build his own measurement systems* (the dashboard check, the CSM spreadsheet). He is not accepting the company's measurement; he is creating a parallel measurement where he is in control. The moment someone creates a measurement system *he cannot parallel* (Marcus's forecast calls with specific three questions about every deal, L13), he feels sick and leaves. So the pattern is not 'leaves all measurement systems'—it is 'stays in systems where he can either control the measurement or create a parallel measurement.' The NICU shatters even this: the nurses have the system in Epic (L24), there is no parallel system he can build that changes the outcome, and he *cannot function* (six minutes, L39). This refines the compounding mechanism: *he can coexist with measurement systems that are either chosen, controllable, or where he can build a better system. When none of those are available, his loyalty collapses and his regulation breaks down.*

evidence.quote: I sent that letter before transfer calls. Two weeks before... And I remember sitting on the floor of the apartment when the calls came through and they read the zone leader assignments and my name wasn't in it, and I felt — this is gonna sound bad — I felt so relaxed.

candidates.falsifier: If he chooses to stay in a leadership role that requires him to be measured by someone else (e.g., joining a larger company as VP, taking an advisor role with board governance), and reports feeling engaged and not sick, this pattern would be challenged. Or if he can sit with Britt for 30 minutes in unstructured conversation without proposing a structure or leaving, this would suggest the mechanism is shifting.
candidates.would_predict: Relationships: If the startup grows to a point where he needs a true co-founder or board, his marriage may become the primary site where he works out the tension between loyalty and autonomy. Britt will either conform to his systems (Council, docs, measurable intimacy) or will escalate her request for unmeasured presence. The outcome will reveal whether he can shift the mechanism: can he be loyal to Britt without needing to measure her, or will he continue to need the system to feel safe? Test case: In the next relationship crisis (a conflict with Britt, a falling-out with an employee, a failed investment decision), observe whether he initiates a conversation or builds a system to contain it. If he builds a system, the pattern is active. If he can sit without structure, the pattern is shifting.

insights.headline: He reads systems in real time and makes them visible through capture (boards, spreadsheets, lists), using external structure as both tool and belonging mechanism—but only when he controls the system.
insights.explanation: The truck (E1: L36-39) establishes the template: father speaks the system aloud; he captures it on clipboard. In Brazil (E2: L19-23), masking-tape grid on apartment door tracks every companionship, every day. At startup (E3: L12-17), dashboard at 5:40 am. In NICU (E5: L20-25), Google Sheet with trend lines. Compounding mechanism surfaces in E5: Britt says 'you'd rather have a meeting with me than a conversation' (L52). He responds by adding 'emotional check-in section' to Council doc (L54)—systematizing the unsystematizable. The genius is capture; the compounding cost is that capture becomes anxiety management, not clarity. He says 'It's the same thing as the fax' (E3: L18) and 'My dad had the truck. I've got the doc' (E5: L58-60)—framing it as inheritance, not coping. When Britt names the pattern, he 'laugh[s], and then I fix the doc' (L52-53)—responding to relational feedback by systematizing further. Only in E4 does capture disappear during decision-making itself (cleaning garage is post-decision ritual, not decision tool), suggesting the mechanism weakens under direct threat to autonomy.

evidence.quote: I made my own board. On the back of our apartment door with masking tape, a grid, every companionship in my district, every day, every number.
It was the fax again. It's the same thing as the fax.

insights.headline: He believes that being measured by someone else's system is unbearable, and he must either control the measure, preempt it, or leave.
insights.explanation: E1: Quits wrestling night before wrestle-off, removing risk of external judgment. Says 'I'd rather be the guy who's building the day than the guy waiting to find out what the day is' (L46)—not preference, but agency. E2: Writes mission letter *before* transfer calls (L43-44)—preemptive control. When calls come and he's not promoted, 'my shoulders came down' (L47) with relief, not disappointment. E4: Seed round offer would mean 'a guy I'd have to call every quarter and explain myself to' (L56-57). Sits in car 40 minutes not thinking about dilution but about the board seat—the *answerability*. Takes lower salary to own 100%. E5: In NICU (zero control, no plan), he 'needed my Google Sheet' (L25) and cannot sit for six minutes (L39). The belief is not stated: *if I don't control the measurement, I will be controlled by it, and this is unbearable.* Preemption is the signature form—quit before wrestle-off, request reassignment before transfer calls, leave before reorg, build company before hierarchical constraint. Agency language shifts to passive when *not* in control: 'They moved it' (E3: L13), 'Marcus came in above me' (E4: L9).

insights.headline: He chooses full ownership and unilateral decision-making authority over advancement, capital, or security—even when it costs him materially and relationally.
insights.explanation: E4 is clearest: refuses seed round with 'decent terms' (L53) that would move company to 4–5M (L58). Reason given is dilution; actual reason is 'a guy I'd have to call every quarter and explain myself to' (L56-57). Takes salary 'honestly less than I was making' (L51); Britt objects ('has thoughts about that'). E2: Preemptively requests tiny Ivaiporã branch when zone leader/assistant available (L32-39). Feels 'relaxed' when not promoted (L45)—relief of unavailability. E1: Quits before wrestle-off he 'still think[s]' he'd have won (L55-57). Chooses truck rides with silent father over varsity. E3: Accepts four promotions passively (not chosen, 'company was doubling, if you just don't leave you go up', L11), responds by building parallel systems of control—not claiming the advancement as his own. This is not regret-free: E5 notes Britt has 'thoughts' about lower salary; E4 notes Sam 'took money and he's at eleven' (L60-61, comparative comparison). But the choices hold. The value surfaces as: *what I control and own matters more than what I achieve within someone else's system.* Not stated, but lived across 4/5 experiences.

evidence.quote: I own a hundred percent of it. A hundred... But I sleep. That's the trade. I sleep.

insights.headline: He believes emotional or relational presence cannot be measured or improved, so he addresses relational rupture through task completion and system building rather than conversation.
insights.explanation: E1: Father never asks why he quit (L43-44); he never brings it up. Connection is not through words but through clipboard (L40: 'closest I ever felt to my dad'). E5: Britt says 'I don't need the numbers. I need you to just sit down' (L36-37). He sits six minutes, then gets coffee for nurses (L40-42). She notes 'you'd rather have a meeting with me than a conversation' (L52); he responds by adding 'emotional check-in section' to doc (L54)—systemizing the unsystematizable. When she cries hard at this, he says 'I still don't totally know which kind of crying that was' (L55)—cannot read the signal. His response to not knowing is not to ask; it is to sit with it without movement, which he cannot do. In NICU: nurses say they 'didn't need' his spreadsheet (L24), but 'I needed my Google Sheet' (L25)—the system is for him, his regulation, not for outcome. He regroutes bathroom at 2 am (L27-29), redoes already-done garage (L31-32). The belief is unspoken: *relational distance is solved by executing a task well, not by being present without frame.* When he cannot measure or task, he either leaves (six minutes) or tasks compulsively (regrouting, bathroom work). No integration of what Britt names (meeting vs. conversation) into his sense-making—he 'laugh[s], and then I fix the doc' (L52-53), suggesting he hears it as solvable problem, not relational request.

insights.headline: He states he values autonomy and hates micromanagement, but systematically tracks, measures, and controls his teams and marriage through external structure—and does not experience this as measurement.
insights.explanation: E3, L20-22: 'I'm a big believer in autonomy. I really am. I hated being micromanaged.' Yet same experience: took Kaylee's account off her, told her it was to help her focus (L31-33). Kaylee's exit cited 'not being trusted' (L36). He says 'that's not what that was' (L36) but does not ask her. Ran every QBR deck himself, rebuilding at 11:40 pm with 'just a couple tweaks!' (L38-42). Built spreadsheet tracking 'every CSM's touches per account per week. Color coded. Nobody asked me for it' (L43-45). E5: Builds Council doc with four pre-set items (L47-48). Britt names it: 'you'd rather have a meeting with me than a conversation' (L52). He responds by adding 'emotional check-in section' (L54)—systematizing further instead of hearing the request. The gap: he experiences being measured (Doug's ride-alongs, Marcus's calls) as invasive and leaves. But when *he* holds the measure, it feels like stewardship. Kaylee and Britt experience micromanagement; he experiences care. The lived version is: *I will not be measured, but I will measure you thoroughly, because measurement is how I show care and keep things legible.* This is distinct from the belief about measurement-anxiety: this is about *who holds the measuring tool*. When he doesn't control it, he's threatened. When he does, it's love.
